speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Government has made important changes to the criminal justice system in recent years, towards a more progressive, balanced and modern criminal justice system that delivers just outcomes and protects society from crime.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Normally, given that all appeals have been exhausted, there will be no further applications possible.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These amendments provide a process for making such applications.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Today, capital cases are governed by a rigorous process with multiple safeguards.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, all persons facing capital charges are offered free legal representation under the Legal Assistance Scheme for Capital Offences, at trial and on appeal.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, capital trials can only be heard in the General Division of the High Court, or HC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The accused can only be found guilty of a capital charge if the Prosecution leads evidence and proves its case at trial, even if the accused does not contest the charge.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, where the HC imposes capital punishment, the accused is entitled to appeal to the Court of Appeal, or CA, against both the conviction and sentence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Even if the accused does not appeal or withdraws his appeal, the CA must still review the case and satisfy itself as to the correctness, legality and propriety of the conviction and sentence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Fourth, even after the CA has confirmed the conviction and sentence, the PACP may apply for the case to be reviewed under Division 1B of Part 20 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2010, or the CPC, if the strict criteria for reviewing a concluded case are met.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under our justice system, a person facing a capital charge has ample opportunity to raise any issues in relation to the charge and the sentence, and to have those issues considered by the Courts at the appropriate time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Our system allows justice to be done, where there are genuine issues to be dealt with.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: After the CA confirms the conviction and sentence, the PACP may also submit a petition to the President for clemency.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In recent years, there have been several instances where PACPs filed last-minute applications in capital cases, after all avenues of appeal have been exhausted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We are introducing this Bill to set out a process for such post-appeal applications in capital cases, to provide more clarity on the applicable court procedure for all parties involved.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the course of finalising the Bill, we consulted the Bar extensively, and took into consideration their feedback, in arriving at the final version of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will now go through the key amendments in the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: A PACC application is an application that meets two criteria.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, the application was made by a PACP after the relevant date, which is either (a) the date when the capital sentence was imposed, upheld or confirmed by the CA, or (b) if there was an earlier application for permission to make a PACC application, or an earlier PACC application, by the PACP that has been decided, the date of the most recent decision.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This makes clear that the new procedure applies to applications filed by a PACP after the appeal in the capital case has concluded or the capital sentence has been confirmed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, either (a) the application is for a stay of execution of the capital sentence, or (b) the determination of the application calls into question, or may call into question, the propriety of the conviction of, the imposition of the capital sentence on, or the carrying out of the capital sentence on, the PACP.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: PACC applications do not include review applications under the CPC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Review applications are applications to review an earlier decision of an appellate court and will continue to be governed by a separate procedure under the CPC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The procedure to apply for the CA’s permission is set out under the new section 60G of the SCJA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In deciding whether to grant permission, the CA is to consider four matters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, whether the intended PACC application is based on material that could not have been adduced in Court before the relevant date, even with reasonable diligence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, whether there was any delay in applying for permission after the material was obtained, and the reasons for the delay.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, whether the prescribed supporting documents have been filed within the prescribed time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These will include supporting affidavit(s) by the PACP’s counsel, or by the PACP, if he is unrepresented.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The affidavit is to state, among others, the grounds for the application and the reasons for not filing the application earlier.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Fourth, whether the intended PACC application has a reasonable prospect of success.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Even if these four matters are not satisfied, the CA will have the discretion to grant permission for the application if it thinks fit.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If permission is granted, the PACC application must then be made to the CA, and fixed for hearing, within the prescribed periods.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The applicable procedure at this stage is set out under the new section 60H of the SCJA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Having the CA directly hear PACC applications provides a streamlined procedure for such applications, while still allowing these applications to be ventilated before the apex court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is provided for under the new section 60I of the SCJA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This ensures that the coram hearing the pending application is fully apprised of all the relevant circumstances or issues that the PACP wishes to raise and is able to deal with the matter holistically.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: When a PACP files any application or action in a Court other than the CA, the new section 60J of the SCJA allows the CA to determine whether the application is, or the action contains, an application for PACC permission or a PACC application.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If it so determines, the CA can deal with the application or action accordingly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The finding may be made on the CA’s own motion or upon the application of the Attorney-General or Public Prosecutor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is in line with the CA’s current powers to make findings of abuse of process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In deciding whether to make a finding of an abuse of process, the CA may take additional evidence, and may inquire into and take into account whether the prescribed matters for the making of a PACC application or a review application have been satisfied.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Lastly, clause 3 provides for amendments to the CPC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These are primarily consequential amendments to align certain aspects of the procedure for review applications with the new procedure for PACC applications in clause 2.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This amendment will provide clarity for all parties on when the sentence may be carried out.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It also provides statutory protection to PACPs by prohibiting the carrying out of the capital sentence – even without a stay of execution – where there is a pending application for permission to apply for a stay of execution, or an application for a stay of execution that meets the specified criteria.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendments will provide greater clarity and guidance on the process and considerations which PACPs and their counsel should have regard to when making post-appeal applications.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendments also do not affect access to justice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for the Minister for Law)
text: PACPs are not prevented from filing their applications and ventilating their arguments in Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the varied considerations do not just include the rights of the condemned prisoner.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are other stakeholders in the criminal justice process.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These include the rights of victims, the demand for fairness in the judicial system and the desire that Singapore remains safe for all.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For a prisoner awaiting capital punishment, the arguments are not academic discussions of principle but, literally, a matter of life and death.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prior to the introduction of this Bill, and after the Government indicated that it was considering introducing post-appeal procedures for capital cases, I authored an op-ed in our local press on the mandatory death penalty.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One point I made was to leave the matter of late applications to the Courts and allow cost orders to be the appropriate sanction.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My concern was that the legislative changes proposed would either significantly curtail or prohibit post-appeal applications.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because of the irreversibility of the death penalty, lawyers should not be unduly fettered from advancing arguments to ensure that justice is done and their clients are saved from the noose.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But I note that new material in the form of evidence and legal arguments are not prohibited by the proposals before the House today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a matter of principle, I do not see this Bill as hampering legal counsel who represent their clients dutifully.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The regulation of the PACC process has come into focus arising from the reality of vexatious applications.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When I say, "come into focus", I am not talking only about the sterile procedural aspects of PACCs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The point here is that PACCs cause profound human effects.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One cannot discount the reality of these applications taking their toll on the prisoner, their spouses, their children, their parents, their extended families and their friends.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the hopes created by PACCs are reasonably achievable hopes, natural justice demands that we do not close any door to them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, in cases of vexatious applications, which have a zero chance of success, then the hopes are wickedly false, if the lawyers are aware of that fact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While these prisoners are persons who have been convicted of crimes and who have exhausted their avenues of appeal, we must do right by them as that reflects what we want to be as a society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If I can sum it up in one word, what most of us want in the system is fairness.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fairness must be a guiding principle in scrutinising all procedures relating to the death penalty.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of course, some may argue that it is not fair at all for the state to take the life of any person.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But that is not the discussion for today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The mandatory death penalty is in our statutes for now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That may change as society or circumstances change.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our purpose today is to look at a sliver of the process and consider the just and fair handling of PACCs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the interest of achieving a fair process for PACCs, I have a few clarifications about the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first clarification relates to the statement made by the MinLaw spokesman and quoted The Straits Times of 7 November.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The spokesman said, and I quote, "The proposed amendments will clearly set out the process for such applications and the Court will have discretion to allow challenges, even if they do not comply with this process".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is the spokesman merely referring to the provisions in the proposed section 60J, under which the Court of Appeal may treat an application in another Court as a PACC application?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If not, could the Senior Parliamentary Secretary clarify?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second clarification concerns the proposed section 60J(7) which provides the matters the Court of Appeal must consider in deciding whether to grant an application for PACC permission.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As such, I would like to clarify if the threshold standard required here is that of an arguable case and if this would represent the legislative intent insofar as section 60G(7)(d) is concerned?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If section 60G(7)(d) is not meant to be a threshold standard but merely a consideration which could possibly be disregarded if an arguable case comes before the Court, I would suggest that this be confirmed in the Senior Parliamentary Secretary's round-up speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My third clarification concerns the phrase "even with reasonable diligence" used in the proposed section 60G(7)(a), section 60G(15)(c) and more than once in section 60M.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My reading is that the use of the word "even" suggests that reasonable diligence is being compared with a higher standard, say due diligence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, then to the extent that it endeavours to set a reachable standard, I do not object to it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the Senior Parliamentary Secretary can clarify this, then, should the Bill be passed, it would make clear to the Court of Appeal the legislative intent is to set a lower standard than that of due diligence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The use of the term "reasonable diligence" brings me to my fourth clarification.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is unless evidence or legal arguments are presented that were not adduced before the finding of abuse of process and evidence or legal arguments could not even with reasonable diligence have been adduced in Court before the finding.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Here, Madam, there is a need to distinguish between the prisoner and the lawyer representing that prisoner.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is possible to conceive of a situation where the lawyer who made the prior application, which was an abuse of process, was not thorough enough in raising evidence or legal arguments that were reasonably available.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prisoner then changes lawyers and the new, more diligent lawyer then raises the evidence and legal arguments which were available previously but not raised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In such a scenario, it would appear that the Court of Appeal will have no discretion to take into consideration such a situation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The remedy against the lawyer who did not raise the arguments could be a personal cost order.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the prisoner should not be unfairly prejudiced.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to hearing the Senior Parliamentary Secretary's responses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Subject to the replies to my queries, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such processes and the grounds for any decisions must be clear and transparent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the powers of the Court of Appeal to take additional evidence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A number of provisions in the Bill allow the Court of Appeal to take additional evidence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These situations include where the Court of Appeal is considering an application for permission to make a PACC application, is hearing a PACC application, is considering whether an application is a PACC application and is determining if there is an abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary clarify whether the Court’s power to take additional evidence is exercisable only of the Court’s own motion or whether a party can apply for the Court to exercise its power to take additional evidence?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary also share on what grounds or in what circumstances will the Court exercise its power to take additional evidence?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If it is open to a party to apply to Court to take additional evidence, can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary clarify on what grounds can the application be made by a party?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is what the standard of reasonable prospect of success entails.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To provide more clarity on what constitutes a “reasonable prospect of success”, can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary share how this standard compares to the other standards articulated by the Court?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on the meaning of abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Court of Appeal also has the power to make a finding of abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the case of Syed Suhail bin Syed Zin vs Attorney-General, the Court found that while the defence counsel brought the review application to acquit Syed of the death penalty, this was by itself insufficient to find a collateral purpose amounting to an abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Court observed that more would be needed to suggest that the intended outcome is in itself an abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary clarify what factors the Court should consider if determining an application is an abuse of process?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would first like to declare that I am a practising lawyer.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The accused persons would then be assigned by the LASCO case assignment panel with a lead counsel with at least seven years of legal practice, who have represented parties in several capital trials and appeals before the Court of Appeal against conviction and trial or acquittal.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Second, an assisting counsel with at least five years of legal practice and have represented parties in capital trials.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And sometimes, also with a junior assisting counsel with experience in criminal trial procedure.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This team of assigned lawyers is expected to put forward the client's instructions to the best of their ability at the earliest opportunity through making representations to the prosecution, in the hope that the charge can be reduced to a non-capital one.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If unsuccessful, they would proceed to put up a strongest possible defence at trial.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the event that the trial judge is not with the defence and finds the accused to be guilty, deliberations will be made whether an appeal ought to be made against the conviction on the basis that the trial judge might have either made an error of law or an error of fact in reaching his decision.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the procedure develops to this stage and beyond, you will often find that the defence case is evidentially weak and chances of succeeding becomes even slimmer.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While counsels might have advised the convicted person on this, the convicted persons may, at times, still insist and instruct his lawyers to explore further court proceeding options.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Grasping at straws, while prolonging their time away from facing the gallows, such futile exercises would invariably cause much time and resources to be wasted.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, I wish to take this opportunity to seek the following clarifications.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Typically, LASCO’s assignment will end in the event mitigation has been made by counsel and sentence has been given by the Court or when the case has been delisted from the Supreme Court – for example, when the prosecution eventually offers to reduce the charge to a non-capital one and be dealt with at the State Court’s jurisdiction instead – or when Presidential clemency has already been sought after the accused has been convicted of the capital offence.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The next question is in relation to whether one, three or five Court of Appeal judges to decide on PACC matters.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Pursuant to the new section 60G(2) of the SCJA, the application for permission may be heard by a single judge exercising the Court of Appeal’s jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The SCJA also empowers for such application to be dealt with by three or any greater uneven number of judges sitting in the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Whilst I understand the efficiency in getting just one Court of Appeal judge to hear and make a decision, we have witnessed on several occasions where landmark cases were made when Court of Appeal judges have dissenting views amongst themselves.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The fact that such application for PACC may constitute a last-ditch attempt to prevent a possibility of miscarriage of justice means it might be prudent to have at least three Court of Appeal judges hear such applications.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the event a single judge has been tasked to decide on the application for permission and/or the PACC application, I understand from the new section 60G(8) and section 60H(6) of the SCJA that such applications may be summarily addressed without an oral hearing.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In such situations where the Court of Appeal judge has refused the application, I hope that a substantive written decision will be given to explain the basis of the decision.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would also suggest that there be liberty for PACP or his/her counsel to write in to seek clarifications and make further submissions to convince the judge otherwise.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As per Lord Hewart, the then Lord Chief Justice of England, “Justice must not only be done, but must also be seen to be done”.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Among other things, the exercise of discretion by the State in scheduling his execution is subject to legal limits, including the usual principles of judicial review and the fundamental liberties protected by the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Those where the words of Justice of Appeal Andrew Phang, a luminary legal giant who was honoured by members of the Judiciary, legal professionals and our greater community in his valedictory reference at the Supreme Court yesterday, which I attended.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When I was just a young law student, I observed a capital case hearing in the old Supreme Court Building – just next door.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It was my first time attending any Court hearing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I was surprised when just before the sentencing, all of us in the courtroom was ordered to stand.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understood it as a mark of respect before the death penalty was handed down.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The entire hearing also showed me how the system upholds the sanctity of life and the important role played by everyone – judges, prosecutors, and defence counsel – before anyone is deprived of his or her life.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It was a moment that I remember till today.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is against this backdrop that I stand to speak today.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, on due process – how the Bill can ensure that the accused or PACP can be assured of due process in PACCs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, on liability of solicitors who are representing PACPs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Third, on what we can do together beyond this Bill to ensure that more awareness can be raised in relation to our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This also means that it will be easier for the scheduling of court hearing on an urgent basis.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, a single judge hearing may give the impression that these PACCs are of lesser importance.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since these PACCs are the PACP's last resort, perhaps we should require more safeguards than just one judge presiding over the PACC hearing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a point made by hon Member Ms Hany Soh too.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the use of virtual hearing and technology, it is not difficult to convene a hearing with coram of two or three judges online.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps it can also be clarified that for PACC of a certain degree of complexity, there can be more than one judge.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To ensure efficiency, guillotine time or specific time limits for oral submissions and page limits for written submissions can be set prior to PACCs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To borrow from the practice of international arbitration, the Courts can also set a memorandum of important issues to be address at the hearing so as to focus the judicial time on pertinent issues of relevance and materiality to the outcome of the PACC.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Separately, given the time-sensitive nature of the PACC, I hope that there will be assurance that such applications shall be heard urgently and that the AGC and its prosecutors will do their utmost best to achieve this as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, on the liability of solicitors representing the PACPs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many defence counsel in these cases are doing it pro bono or on LASCO scheme.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are playing an important part in our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We owe a debt of gratitude to them appreciate their key role and contributions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Inevitably, the role of counsel comes under the spotlight in PACC applications where there tend be an abuse of process of delay in making such applications.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, not all blame lies on the solicitor.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Take for example, in cases where counsel has already advised the PACP that the chance of success is low, but the PACP insists on making such an application.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In such a case, I hope that it will be made clear that any costs liability will be borne by the PACP and not counsel, except in egregious abuse of process cases caused by the solicitors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The imposition of personal cost orders against counsel comes under the Criminal Procedure Code whereby lawyers who file applications that are frivolous or vexatious or otherwise an abuse of the process of the Court may have cost sanctions imposed on them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the Court of Appeal in the recent case of Iskandar bin Rahmat has recently held that a high threshold must be met before adverse cost orders may be imposed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the future perhaps the Ministry can consider codifying the narrow situations in which costs penalty may be considered against any counsel for clarity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another scenario is where new solicitors have just taken over conduct of the matter.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some PACPs are known to discharge solicitors and engage new ones at the last moment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In such cases, costs liability should be on the PACP.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because counsel would be place in the most difficult position at the cost submissions or hearing because he or she cannot divulge or breach solicitor-client privilege.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Where the PACCs are not conducted on a pro bono basis or on LASCO, a suggestion perhaps is to require the PACP to furnish security or undertaking for costs if certain requirements are met.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is nothing new in the civil appellate practice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope these suggestions will encourage more defence counsel and pro bono LASCO lawyers who will step forward to contribute.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, I also note the United Nations Human Rights Office of the Commissioner issued a statement in 1984 on the safeguards guaranteeing protection of the rights of those facing the death penalty.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In particular, paragraph 6 of the safeguards stated that steps should be taken to ensure that appeals from a death sentence shall become mandatory.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Paragraph 8 states: "Capital punishment shall not be carried out pending any appeal or other recourse procedure or other proceeding relating to pardon or commutation of the sentence".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we can do more to raise awareness of the approach towards capital offences in our jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For foreign PACPs, what are the measures that can be done to engage foreign embassies and governments on our approach towards PACPs who are foreign citizens?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On a people-to-people level, what more can be done to raise such awareness?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One suggestion, perhaps, would be for our law schools or even the Judiciary to host foreign law students on exchange and expose them to the inner workings of criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that the foreign students or delegation will, having seen us up close, can better understand Singapore's context and criminal justice system on such capital offences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Court retains discretion to grant permission even if any or all the matters are not met.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Bill sets out the conditions to be satisfied and the procedures to be followed and is enabling in nature.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is to advance the interests of justice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The statement by the spokesman referred to by Mr Singh, made the point that ultimately the Court will retain some discretion because the Bill does not absolutely rule out the exercise of such discretion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Parliament's intention is that such applications where the conditions in this Bill have not been satisfied should generally not succeed given the legislative intent expressed through the Bill to set up a process to be followed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Court will exercise considerable care because there is finality, because we do not want to rule out the possibility.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The framework sets out what the Court will consider and it is likely to be extremely rare for the Court to go beyond this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, the intention is for the framework to be followed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Singh had a second question on the point of "must not" in section 60G(15).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The provision on abuse is about abuse by the applicant, not by the lawyer.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: When they have previously abused the process, we think that section 60G(15) is a fair requirement because the Court can still grant permission if the requirements in section 60G(15)(c) and (d) are met, which are reasonable requirements.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On the third point about reasonable diligence, this is a factor for the Courts to consider when deciding whether the evidence and arguments in the application could have been brought earlier.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And this is not a new requirement – it is already in Division 1B of the CPC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Louis Ng had asked whether the Court's power to take additional evidence can only be exercised on its own motion and about the grounds on which the Court would exercise this power.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Court has discretion to decide whether to take additional evidence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Depending on the facts, possible matters that the Court may take into account could include the nature of the additional evidence and its relevance to the issues before the Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ultimately, this is a matter of judicial discretion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Ng had also asked for more clarity on the meaning of the "reasonable prospect of success", which Mr Pritam Singh also touched on.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The phrase "reasonable prospect of success" is meant to clarify that in deciding whether to grant permission to make a PACC application, the CA is to consider the merits of the intended PACC application.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, as the phrase makes clear, the CA is not required to conduct a full determination of the merits when deciding whether to grant permission to make a PACC application.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ultimately, the CA will be guided by the language of the provision, which is whether the intended PACC application has a reasonable prospect of success.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: To this end, it may not be helpful to focus on the standards mentioned by Mr Ng because these have been developed in different contexts and it may not be applicable to the PACC application.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Moreover, as I mentioned earlier, the CA has the discretion to grant permission to make a PACC application even if the CA is not satisfied that the intended PACC application has a reasonable prospect of success.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Ng had also asked for clarification on the factors that the Court should consider when determining whether an application is an abuse of process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The new section 60M(2) of the SCJA sets out, non-exhaustively, some matters that the Court may take into account in deciding whether to make a finding of abuse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, the Court may consider whether the application is based on material that could not have been adduced before the relevant date, even with reasonable diligence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Hany Soh and Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim raised questions about the coram for applications for PACC permission.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: A PACC application cannot be heard and determined by a single Judge.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Only an application for permission to make a PACC application can be heard and determined by a single Judge.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Having a single Judge hear the application for permission to make a PACC application reflects the fact that, at this stage, the Court is only deciding whether permission to make the PACC application should be granted, and the Court is not required to conduct a full determination of the merits of the PACC application.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In a related vein, under the existing section 394H of the CPC, an application for permission to make a review application in respect of a decision of the CA is to be heard by a single judge sitting in the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Further, even in the case of an application for permission to make a PACC application, the CA has discretion in each matter whether to convene a coram of three Judges or a greater uneven number of Judges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Depending on the facts, a possible matter that the Court may take into account could be an issue raised in the application.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And ultimately, this is a matter of judicial discretion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain offered some suggestions to ensure the efficient use of judicial time for PACC applications.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And as to Mr Zhulkarnain's point about the time-sensitive nature of such applications, the cases have shown that the Courts hear them urgently.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Hany Soh asked about the written grounds of decision and whether the applicant can seek clarifications and make further submissions after applications are summarily dismissed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The CA has discretion to decide whether it will issue a judgment or grounds of decision together with or following the issuance of the written order.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Any consequential matters raised will be dealt with by the CA.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Soh had also asked about whether LASCO will be extended to cover PACC applications.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Any such extension will have to be carefully studied in consultation with the relevant stakeholders before a decision is taken.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked about costs orders against lawyers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: All lawyers have a duty to conscientiously assess the merits of a case before engaging in court proceedings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If the lawyer thinks there is no merit but the PACP insists on making the application, the lawyer should decline to act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Courts have observed that the filing of ill-considered and baseless applications by lawyers cannot be justified on the basis that the PACP faces a capital sentence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are well-established principles on when a personal costs order can be made against a lawyer.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is for the Courts, in the exercise of judicial discretion, to determine whether to make a personal costs order against a lawyer.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In such cases, the lawyer will have the opportunity to be heard.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain has highlighted the importance of raising international awareness and understanding of Singapore's approach to capital offences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Criticisms of Singapore's approach are often based on misconceptions and inaccurate facts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Singapore actively engages in international fora such as the UN, as well as bilaterally to address misconceptions and explain our approach.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will continue to engage and raise awareness and I thank Mr Zhulkarnain for his suggestions on how we can do so.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I believe I have answered the questions raised by the Members.
